claim: Telomere shortening is a presumed tumor suppressor pathway that imposes a proliferative barrier (the Hayflick limit) during tumorigenesis.
source: Telomere shortening is a presumed tumor suppressor pathway that imposes a proliferative barrier (the Hayflick limit) during tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific theory about telomere function in cancer prevention.

claim: Excessively long somatic telomeres predispose to cancer.
source: This model predicts that excessively long somatic telomeres predispose to cancer.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the telomere tumor suppressor model.

claim: Cancer-prone families have two unique TINF2 mutations that truncate TIN2.
source: Here, we describe cancer-prone families with two unique TINF2 mutations that truncate TIN2, a shelterin subunit that controls telomere length.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic analysis and sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patient lymphocyte telomeres were unusually long.
source: Patient lymphocyte telomeres were unusually long.
evidence: This is supported by Flow-FISH and genomic blotting data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The truncated TIN2 proteins do not localize to telomeres.
source: We show that the truncated TIN2 proteins do not localize to telomeres, suggesting that the mutations create loss-of-function alleles.
evidence: This is supported by telomeric ChIP and immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TINF2 mutations create loss-of-function alleles.
source: We show that the truncated TIN2 proteins do not localize to telomeres, suggesting that the mutations create loss-of-function alleles.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of telomere localization and functional studies.

claim: Heterozygous knock-in of the mutations resulted in excessive telomere elongation in clonal lines.
source: Heterozygous knock-in of the mutations or deletion of one copy of TINF2 resulted in excessive telomere elongation in clonal lines, indicating that TINF2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control.
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis in CRISPR-edited cell lines shown in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of one copy of TINF2 resulted in excessive telomere elongation in clonal lines.
source: Heterozygous knock-in of the mutations or deletion of one copy of TINF2 resulted in excessive telomere elongation in clonal lines, indicating that TINF2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control.
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis in CRISPR-edited cell lines shown in the manuscript.

claim: TINF2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control.
source: Heterozygous knock-in of the mutations or deletion of one copy of TINF2 resulted in excessive telomere elongation in clonal lines, indicating that TINF2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control.
evidence: This is concluded from the telomere elongation phenotype observed in heterozygous cells.

claim: Telomere protection and genome stability were maintained in all heterozygous clones.
source: In contrast, telomere protection and genome stability were maintained in all heterozygous clones.
evidence: This is supported by TIF assays and metaphase spread analysis showing no increase in telomere dysfunction.

claim: The TINF2 truncations predispose to a tumor syndrome.
source: The data establish that the TINF2 truncations predispose to a tumor syndrome.
evidence: This is concluded from the clinical data showing multiple malignancies in families with TINF2 mutations.

claim: TINF2 acts as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor that limits telomere length to ensure a timely Hayflick limit.
source: We conclude that TINF2 acts as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor that limits telomere length to ensure a timely Hayflick limit.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined genetic, cellular, and clinical data.

claim: Telomeres shorten in normal human cells.
source: The idea that telomere attrition could repress the outgrowth of early stage cancer originates from the observation that telomeres shorten in normal human cells (Harley et al., 1990; Hastie et al., 1990; de Lange et al., 1990; reviewed in Maciejowski and de Lange, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Telomere shortening leads to a proliferative barrier in vitro (the Hayflick limit).
source: In agreement with this theory, telomere shortening leads to a proliferative barrier in vitro (the Hayflick limit Shay and Wright, 2000) that can be overcome when telomerase is activated through expression of hTERT Bodnar et al., 1998
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Hayflick limit can be overcome when telomerase is activated through expression of hTERT.
source: In agreement with this theory, telomere shortening leads to a proliferative barrier in vitro (the Hayflick limit Shay and Wright, 2000) that can be overcome when telomerase is activated through expression of hTERT Bodnar et al., 1998
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Telomerase activity is required to create tumorigenic derivatives from normal human cells.
source: telomerase activity is required to create tumorigenic derivatives from normal human cells Hahn et al., 1999
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Telomerase activation is a hallmark of human cancer.
source: and telomerase activation is a hallmark of human cancer (Shay and Bacchetti, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: hTERT promoter mutations were discovered in familial melanoma and other tumor types.
source: The discovery of hTERT promoter mutations in familial melanoma and other tumor types further solidified the view that telomere attrition is a barrier to tumorigenesis (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013; reviewed in Lorbeer and Hockemeyer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Telomeres shorten at a rate of ~30–100 bp/end/cell division in most primary human cells.
source: For the telomere tumor suppression pathway to limit cancer incidence, telomeres need to shorten at the correct rate, which in most primary human cells is ~30–100 bp/end/cell division (Harley et al., 1990; Huffman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The number of cell divisions a transformed clone can execute before proliferation is curbed depends on the initial telomere length.
source: The number of cell divisions a transformed clone can execute before proliferation is curbed by one or more critically short telomeres depends on the initial telomere length.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between telomere length and replicative capacity.

claim: The lengths of the shortest telomeres in a clone determine its proliferative potential.
source: Most likely, it is the lengths of the shortest telomeres in a clone that determine its proliferative potential (Hemann et al., 2001; Zou et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Excessive telomere length at birth will delay the Hayflick limit and create a permissive state for cancer development.
source: These considerations predict that excessive telomere length at birth will delay the Hayflick limit and create a permissive state for cancer development.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the telomere tumor suppressor model.

claim: A cancer cell line with very long telomeres remained tumorigenic until its telomere reserve was depleted after removal of telomerase.
source: Indeed, after removal of telomerase, a cancer cell line with very long telomeres remained tumorigenic until its telomere reserve was depleted (Taboski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Human telomeres have an average length at birth that is specific to our species.
source: At birth, human telomeres have an average length that is specific to our species (Kipling and Cooke, 1990; Gomes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The telomere reserve is sufficient to sustain cell division needed for normal development and tissue homeostasis but becomes depleted during over-proliferation associated with tumorigenesis.
source: It is thought that this telomere reserve is sufficient to sustain the cell division needed for normal development and tissue homeostasis but becomes depleted during the over-proliferation associated with tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on the telomere tumor suppressor model.

claim: Telomere length homeostasis is mediated by shelterin in telomerase-positive tissue culture cells.
source: In telomerase-positive tissue culture cells, telomere length homeostasis is mediated by shelterin (reviewed in Hockemeyer and Collins, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: TIN2 is a central component in shelterin that binds to three other shelterin subunits.
source: TIN2 is a central component in shelterin that binds to three other shelterin subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about shelterin structure.

claim: TIN2 interacts with both TRF1 and TRF2.
source: TIN2 interacts with both double-stranded telomeric DNA-binding proteins – TRF1 and TRF2 – and binds TPP1, which forms a heterodimer with the single-stranded telomeric DNA-binding protein POT1 (reviewed in de Lange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: TIN2 binds TPP1, which forms a heterodimer with POT1.
source: TIN2 interacts with both double-stranded telomeric DNA-binding proteins – TRF1 and TRF2 – and binds TPP1, which forms a heterodimer with the single-stranded telomeric DNA-binding protein POT1 (reviewed in de Lange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: TIN2 has been implicated as a negative regulator of telomere length.
source: TIN2 has been implicated as negative regulator of telomere length as have TRF1 and POT1 (van Steensel and de Lange, 1997; Kim et al., 1999; Loayza and De Lange, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: TRF1 has been implicated as a negative regulator of telomere length.
source: TIN2 has been implicated as negative regulator of telomere length as have TRF1 and POT1 (van Steensel and de Lange, 1997; Kim et al., 1999; Loayza and De Lange, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: POT1 has been implicated as a negative regulator of telomere length.
source: TIN2 has been implicated as negative regulator of telomere length as have TRF1 and POT1 (van Steensel and de Lange, 1997; Kim et al., 1999; Loayza and De Lange, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The current model for telomere length homeostasis invokes a negative feedback loop wherein telomerase is inhibited in cis by proteins that accumulate on TTAGGG repeats.
source: The current model for telomere length homeostasis invokes a negative feedback loop, wherein telomerase is inhibited in cis by proteins (e.g. TRF1, TIN2, and POT1) that accumulate on the TTAGGG repeats synthesized by the enzyme.
evidence: This is a statement of the current theoretical model in the field.

claim: When telomeres are too short at birth, dyskeratosis congenita and related syndromes can arise.
source: It is well established that when telomeres are too short at birth, a devastating bone-marrow failure syndrome (dyskeratosis congenita [DC] and related syndromes) can arise.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC.

claim: Missense mutations in the DC patch of TIN2 are responsible for ~25% of DC cases.
source: Missense mutations in a short stretch of amino acids of TIN2 (the DC patch) are responsible for ~25% of DC cases (Savage et al., 2008; Walne et al., 2008; reviewed in Savage and Bertuch, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The majority of DC cases are due to mutations impinging on telomerase biogenesis and activity.
source: whereas the majority of DC cases are due to mutations impinging on telomerase biogenesis and activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC etiology.

claim: Inherited POT1 mutations in cancer-prone families are associated with excessively long telomeres in somatic cells.
source: Inherited POT1 mutations in cancer-prone families are associated with excessively long telomeres in somatic cells (Robles-Espinoza et al., 2014; NCI DCEG Cancer Sequencing Working Group et al., 2014; reviewed in Gong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: POT1 mutations lead to genome instability.
source: However, the POT1 mutations also lead to genome instability, which has been invoked as the main pathogenic determinant (Ramsay et al., 2013; Pinzaru et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: POT1 mutations have not provided unambiguous evidence for the idea that long telomeres predispose to cancer.
source: Therefore, the POT1 mutations have not provided unambiguous evidence for the idea that long telomeres predispose to cancer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the existing literature on POT1 mutations.

claim: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TINF2 exist in cancer-prone families.
source: Here, we describe heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TINF2 in cancer-prone families.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TINF2 mutations do not compromise telomere protection.
source: These mutations do not compromise telomere protection but create excessively long telomeres in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by TIF assays and metaphase spread analysis.

claim: The TINF2 mutations create excessively long telomeres in vitro and in vivo.
source: These mutations do not compromise telomere protection but create excessively long telomeres in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by telomere length measurements in patient cells and cell lines.

claim: The affected individuals are cancer-prone because their overly long telomeres thwart the telomere tumor suppressor pathway.
source: We conclude that the affected individuals are cancer-prone because their overly long telomeres thwart the telomere tumor suppressor pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined data.

claim: Whole-exome sequencing was performed on lymphocyte DNA of patients who developed multiple malignancies and/or had a striking family history of cancer.
source: In a routine diagnostic setting, whole-exome sequencing was performed on lymphocyte DNA of patients who developed multiple malignancies and/or had a striking family history of cancer.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to identify the mutations.

claim: Germline variants in exon 5 of TINF2 were discovered in four probands.
source: Germline variants in exon 5 of TINF2 (encoding TIN2) were discovered in four probands (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data and pedigree analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Three probands shared the c.604G > C mutation.
source: Three probands shared c.604G > C, whereas the fourth carried c.557del.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: One proband carried the c.557del mutation.
source: Three probands shared c.604G > C, whereas the fourth carried c.557del.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The six individuals in this study developed 14 malignancies.
source: The six individuals in this study developed 14 malignancies (Figure 1A), including three papillary thyroid carcinomas, three breast carcinomas, and two melanomas (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is documented in the clinical data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The malignancies included three papillary thyroid carcinomas, three breast carcinomas, and two melanomas.
source: The six individuals in this study developed 14 malignancies (Figure 1A), including three papillary thyroid carcinomas, three breast carcinomas, and two melanomas (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is documented in the clinical data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: No loss of heterozygosity was detected in six tumors tested.
source: No loss of heterozygosity was detected in six tumors tested and second hits in TINF2 were excluded in four of the six tumors analyzed by whole-exome sequencing (F3:III-1; Astrocytoma, F2:II-1; Melanoma and breast cancer, F1:II-4; colorectal cancer (CRC), see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor sequencing data.

claim: Second hits in TINF2 were excluded in four of the six tumors analyzed by whole-exome sequencing.
source: No loss of heterozygosity was detected in six tumors tested and second hits in TINF2 were excluded in four of the six tumors analyzed by whole-exome sequencing (F3:III-1; Astrocytoma, F2:II-1; Melanoma and breast cancer, F1:II-4; colorectal cancer (CRC), see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor sequencing data.

claim: Multiple somatic driver mutations were identified in the tumors, all previously associated with the tumor type.
source: Multiple somatic driver mutations were identified, all previously associated with the tumor type in which the mutation was identified, such as BRAF (c.1799T > A, p.Val600Glu) in CRC and melanoma, and PIK3CA (c.1624G > A, p.Glu542Lys) in breast cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BRAF (c.1799T > A, p.Val600Glu) mutations were found in CRC and melanoma.
source: Multiple somatic driver mutations were identified, all previously associated with the tumor type in which the mutation was identified, such as BRAF (c.1799T > A, p.Val600Glu) in CRC and melanoma, and PIK3CA (c.1624G > A, p.Glu542Lys) in breast cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PIK3CA (c.1624G > A, p.Glu542Lys) mutations were found in breast cancer.
source: Multiple somatic driver mutations were identified, all previously associated with the tumor type in which the mutation was identified, such as BRAF (c.1799T > A, p.Val600Glu) in CRC and melanoma, and PIK3CA (c.1624G > A, p.Glu542Lys) in breast cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tumors did not reveal a shared somatic mutational spectrum.
source: The tumors did not reveal a shared somatic mutational spectrum (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the tumor sequencing data.

claim: Carriers of the reported TINF2 variants might benefit from regular thyroid and dermatological surveillance as well as more general cancer surveillance.
source: Based on these families, we suggest that carriers of the reported TINF2 variants might benefit from regular thyroid and dermatological surveillance as well as more general cancer surveillance.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the observed cancer spectrum.

claim: The c.557del mutation creates a shift in the reading frame after serine 186 that ends in a stop codon 23 amino acids downstream.
source: The c.557del mutation creates a shift in the reading frame after serine 186 that ends in a stop codon 23 amino acids downstream (p.(Ser186fs); Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The c.604G > C change disrupts the splice donor site of exon 5.
source: The c.604G > C change disrupts the splice donor site of exon 5 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Patient samples contain an alternative transcript (604G > C II) that lacks exon 5 and contains 20 extra nucleotides from intron 4.
source: Transcript analysis showed that in addition to the wild-type full-length transcript (ENST00000399423.8) and a transcript lacking exons 4 and 5 (ENST00000626689.2), patient samples contain an alternative transcript (604G > C II, Figure 2A,B). Transcript c.604G > C II lacks exon 5 and contains 20 extra nucleotides from intron 4.
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The alternative transcript 604G > C II appears to arise from an alternative splice donor site in intron four with a good splice site consensus score.
source: It appears to arise from an alternative splice donor site in intron four with a good splice site consensus score (alt D4; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis and splice site prediction shown in Figure 2.

claim: Heterozygous RPE1 cells carrying the c.604G > C change contained a second allele-specific transcript (c.604G > C I).
source: In addition, the +/c.604G > C RPE1 cells contained a second allele-specific transcript (c.604G > C I, Figure 2B) generated through an alternative donor site in intron five that bears a good splice site consensus sequence (alt D5; Figure 2B,C and see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 below).
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The c.604G > C I transcript is generated through an alternative donor site in intron five.
source: In addition, the +/c.604G > C RPE1 cells contained a second allele-specific transcript (c.604G > C I, Figure 2B) generated through an alternative donor site in intron five that bears a good splice site consensus sequence (alt D5; Figure 2B,C and see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 below).
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The use of alt D5 results in the addition of 17 nucleotides from intron 5.
source: The use of alt D5 results in the addition of 17 nucleotides from intron 5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The c.604G > C I transcript was most likely missed in the analysis of patient samples due to its lower abundance and co-migration with the wild-type full-length transcript.
source: This transcript was most likely missed in the analysis of the patient samples due to its lower abundance and co-migration with the wild-type full-length transcript.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcript analysis results.

claim: The c.604G > C I and c.604G > C II transcripts both have a frameshift in the TIN2 ORF and are predicted to encode truncated proteins.
source: The c.604G > C I and c.604G > C II transcripts both have a frameshift in the TIN2 ORF and are predicted to encode truncated proteins (p.(L170fs) and p.(E202fs)) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The truncated forms of TIN2 lost the ability to bind to TRF1.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation from 293T cells co-transfected with HA-tagged TIN2 versions and myc-tagged TRF1 showed that, as expected, the truncated forms of TIN2 had lost the ability to bind to TRF1 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction with TRF2 was preserved in the c.604G > C derived E202fs truncation.
source: The interaction with TRF2 was preserved in the c.604G > C derived E202fs truncation and was apparently enhanced in the c.557del-derived S186fs truncation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction with TRF2 was apparently enhanced in the c.557del-derived S186fs truncation.
source: The interaction with TRF2 was preserved in the c.604G > C derived E202fs truncation and was apparently enhanced in the c.557del-derived S186fs truncation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The c.604G > C L170fs protein showed very little (or no) interaction with TRF2.
source: In contrast, the c.604G > C L170fs protein showed very little (or no) interaction with TRF2 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction with TPP1 was preserved in the E202fs version of TIN2.
source: The interaction with TPP1 was preserved in the E202fs version of TIN2 but not in the two other truncated forms (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction with TPP1 was not preserved in the S186fs and L170fs truncated forms.
source: The interaction with TPP1 was preserved in the E202fs version of TIN2 but not in the two other truncated forms (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The localization of TIN2 to telomeres is primarily determined by its ability to interact with TRF1.
source: Since the localization of TIN2 to telomeres is primarily determined by its ability to interact with TRF1 (Frescas and de Lange, 2014), it is expected that the truncated proteins fail to efficiently accumulate at telomeres.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The S186fs and L170fs proteins do not associate with telomeric DNA.
source: In agreement, telomeric ChIP assays using the HA antibody on chromatin from 293T cells expressing the HA-tagged versions of TIN2 showed that the S186fs and L170fs proteins do not associate with telomeric DNA (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by telomeric ChIP data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The E202fs protein may be slightly more proficient in telomeric association but the fraction of telomeric DNA recovered in the ChIP was not significantly increased compared to cells transfected with the empty vector.
source: The E202fs protein may be slightly more proficient in telomeric association but the fraction of telomeric DNA recovered in the ChIP was not significantly increased compared to cells transfected with the empty vector.
evidence: This is based on telomeric ChIP data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The truncated versions of TIN2 have lost the ability to function at telomeres.
source: These data indicate that the truncated versions of TIN2 have lost the ability to function at telomeres.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP and co-IP data.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to knock in the c.557del and c.604G > C mutations in RPE1-hTERT cells deficient for Rb and p53.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to knock in the c.557del and c.604G > C mutations in RPE1-hTERT cells deficient for Rb and p53 (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology used to generate the cell lines.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 editing was designed to generate matched wild-type control clones.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 editing was designed to generate matched wild-type control clones with TINF2 genes that were either unedited or edited with silent nucleotide changes (introduction of a restriction enzyme site and a mutated PAM).
evidence: This describes the methodology used to generate control cell lines.

claim: Heterozygous KO clones (TIN2+/KO or +/-) were generated by targeting exon 1 of TINF2.
source: In addition, we targeted exon 1 of TINF2 to generate heterozygous KO clones (TIN2+/KO or +/-; Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and accompanying control clones.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to generate knockout cell lines.

claim: Several clones with the desired alterations were isolated for each genotype.
source: For each genotype, several clones with the desired alterations were isolated (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mutated clonal cell lines showed the same proliferation rate as the control clones.
source: The mutated clonal cell lines showed the same proliferation rate as the control clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 editing of RPE1 cells yielded a viable clone homozygous for the c.604G > C mutation.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 editing of RPE1 cells also yielded a viable clone homozygous for the c.604G > C mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Transcript analysis of the heterozygous and homozygous c.604G > C RPE1 clones confirmed expression of the c.604G > C II mRNA identified in patient samples.
source: Transcript analysis of the heterozygous and homozygous c.604G > C RPE1 clones confirmed expression of the c.604G > C II mRNA identified in patient samples (see Figure 2A,B) and identified the c.604G > C I transcript as an additional product from the mutated locus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by transcript analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Clones heterozygous for the c.604G > C or c.557del mutation and the TIN2+/- clones had slightly lower TIN2 protein levels relative to the controls.
source: Clones heterozygous for the c.604G > C or c.557del mutation and the TIN2+/- clones had slightly lower TIN2 protein levels relative to the controls (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Cells heterozygous for the mutations retained TIN2, TRF1, TPP1, and POT1 at their telomeres.
source: Based on telomeric chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and immunofluorescence (IF) analysis, cells heterozygous for the mutations retained TIN2, TRF1, TPP1, and POT1 at their telomeres, although the data do not exclude a moderate reduction in the association of these proteins with telomeres (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B–G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and IF data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The homozygous c.604G > C clone showed a complete absence of TIN2 in immunoblots.
source: In contrast, the homozygous c.604G > C clone showed a complete absence of TIN2 in immunoblots and the presence of TIN2, TRF1, TPP1, and POT1 at telomeres was strongly reduced (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and ChIP/IF data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of TIN2, TRF1, TPP1, and POT1 at telomeres was strongly reduced in the homozygous c.604G > C clone.
source: In contrast, the homozygous c.604G > C clone showed a complete absence of TIN2 in immunoblots and the presence of TIN2, TRF1, TPP1, and POT1 at telomeres was strongly reduced (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and IF data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Clones with heterozygous c.557del or c.604G > C mutations had the same TIF response as the control cells.
source: Clones with heterozygous c.557del or c.604G > C mutations had the same TIF response as the control cells (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by TIF assay data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The TIF response was not increased in the TIN2+/- clones compared to wild-type controls.
source: Similarly, the TIF response was not increased in the TIN2+/- clones compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: This is supported by TIF assay data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The homozygous c.604G > C clone showed obvious loss of telomere protection.
source: In contrast, the homozygous c.604G > C clone showed obvious loss of telomere protection (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 6A), likely due to the reduced telomeric association of POT1, which is required to prevent the activation of ATR signaling at human telomeres (Denchi and de Lange, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by TIF assay data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The loss of telomere protection in the homozygous c.604G > C clone is likely due to the reduced telomeric association of POT1.
source: In contrast, the homozygous c.604G > C clone showed obvious loss of telomere protection (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 6A), likely due to the reduced telomeric association of POT1, which is required to prevent the activation of ATR signaling at human telomeres (Denchi and de Lange, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of POT1 and the observed reduction in POT1 at telomeres.

claim: POT1 is required to prevent the activation of ATR signaling at human telomeres.
source: In contrast, the homozygous c.604G > C clone showed obvious loss of telomere protection (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 6A), likely due to the reduced telomeric association of POT1, which is required to prevent the activation of ATR signaling at human telomeres (Denchi and de Lange, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: One functional TINF2 gene is sufficient to sustain full telomere protection.
source: These results indicate that one functional TINF2 gene is sufficient to sustain full telomere protection and that the truncated TIN2 proteins do not have a dominant negative effect on telomere protection.
evidence: This is concluded from the TIF assay data showing no increase in telomere dysfunction in heterozygous cells.

claim: The truncated TIN2 proteins do not have a dominant negative effect on telomere protection.
source: These results indicate that one functional TINF2 gene is sufficient to sustain full telomere protection and that the truncated TIN2 proteins do not have a dominant negative effect on telomere protection.
evidence: This is concluded from the TIF assay data showing no increase in telomere dysfunction in heterozygous cells.

claim: Heterozygosity for the TINF2 mutations or the exon 1 KO allele did not induce a significant level of telomere dysfunction.
source: Similarly, analysis of metaphase spreads showed that heterozygosity for the TINF2 mutations or the exon 1 KO allele did not induce a significant level of telomere dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by metaphase spread analysis shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Cells carrying the homozygous c.604G > C mutation showed elevated levels of sister telomere associations and a low level of chromosome fusions.
source: Although cells carrying the homozygous c.604G > C mutation showed elevated levels of sister telomere associations and a low level of chromosome fusions, such aberrations were not significantly increased in the heterozygous clones relative to wild type (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by metaphase spread analysis shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Sister telomere associations and chromosome fusions were not significantly increased in the heterozygous clones relative to wild type.
source: Although cells carrying the homozygous c.604G > C mutation showed elevated levels of sister telomere associations and a low level of chromosome fusions, such aberrations were not significantly increased in the heterozygous clones relative to wild type (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by metaphase spread analysis shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: TINF2 is not haploinsufficient for telomere protection.
source: Thus, TINF2 is not haploinsufficient for telomere protection and the TINF2 mutations are unlikely to induce cancer-promoting genome rearrangements.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of telomere dysfunction in heterozygous cells.

claim: The TINF2 mutations are unlikely to induce cancer-promoting genome rearrangements.
source: Thus, TINF2 is not haploinsufficient for telomere protection and the TINF2 mutations are unlikely to induce cancer-promoting genome rearrangements.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of genome instability in heterozygous cells.

claim: Telomere length analysis in lymphocytes from three patients carrying the c.604G > C or c.557del mutations revealed a median telomere length above the 99th percentile as measured by Flow-FISH.
source: Telomere length analysis in lymphocytes from three patients carrying the c.604G > C or c.557del mutations revealed a median telomere length above the 99th percentile as measured by Flow-FISH (Figure 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Flow-FISH data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Individuals with the TINF2 p.W198fs mutation showed telomeres that were approximately twofold longer based on qPCR.
source: Similarly, individuals with the TINF2 p.W198fs mutation showed telomeres that were approximately twofold longer based on qPCR (He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Primary and EBV-immortalized lymphocytes from two patients carried telomeres of ~13 kb.
source: The presence of exceptionally long telomeres in the c.604G > C individuals was verified by genomic blotting, showing that both primary and EBV-immortalized lymphocytes from two patients carried telomeres of ~13 kb (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic blotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Telomere elongation was observed in RPE1 clones heterozygous for c.557del or c.604G > C.
source: Consistent with the unusually long telomeres in the patients, telomere elongation was observed in RPE1 clones heterozygous for c.557del or c.604G > C (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis shown in Figure 5B-F.

claim: Both the c.557del and the c.604G > C mutation resulted in a greater extension of the telomeres compared to control clones.
source: Comparison of the telomere elongation per PD between the control clones and the heterozygous clones showed that both the c.557del and the c.604G > C mutation resulted in a greater extension of the telomeres (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis shown in Figure 5B-F.

claim: Cells heterozygous for the exon one truncation showed greater rates of telomere elongation.
source: Similarly, cells heterozygous for the exon one truncation showed greater rates of telomere elongation and this phenotype was observed in RPE1 cells as well as in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) heterozygous for a deletion of exons 4–7 (Figure 5G–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: hESCs heterozygous for a deletion of exons 4–7 showed greater rates of telomere elongation.
source: Similarly, cells heterozygous for the exon one truncation showed greater rates of telomere elongation and this phenotype was observed in RPE1 cells as well as in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) heterozygous for a deletion of exons 4–7 (Figure 5G–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by telomere length analysis shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: All RPE1 clones showed approximately the same telomerase activity.
source: All RPE1 clones showed approximately the same telomerase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed telomere elongation is likely due to telomerase-mediated elongation.
source: The observed telomere elongation is likely due to telomerase-mediated elongation because there was no evidence for increased telomere recombination in the cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and the telomeres did not show the typical heterogeneous size of ALT telomeres (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increased T-SCE and the uniform telomere length distribution.

claim: There was no evidence for increased telomere recombination in the cell lines.
source: The observed telomere elongation is likely due to telomerase-mediated elongation because there was no evidence for increased telomere recombination in the cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and the telomeres did not show the typical heterogeneous size of ALT telomeres (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by T-SCE analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The telomeres did not show the typical heterogeneous size of ALT telomeres.
source: The observed telomere elongation is likely due to telomerase-mediated elongation because there was no evidence for increased telomere recombination in the cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and the telomeres did not show the typical heterogeneous size of ALT telomeres (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the telomere length distribution shown in Figure 5.

claim: An effect of TIN2 on telomerase-mediated telomere elongation is consistent with prior data showing that a truncated TIN2 protein induced dramatic telomere elongation in cells expressing telomerase but had no effect in telomerase-negative cells.
source: An effect of TIN2 on telomerase-mediated telomere elongation is consistent with prior data showing that a truncated TIN2 protein induced dramatic telomere elongation in cells expressing telomerase but had no effect in telomerase-negative cells (Kim et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The TINF2 gene is haploinsufficient for telomere length control.
source: These data indicate that the TINF2 gene is haploinsufficient for telomere length control and explain the telomere elongation phenotype in the patients.
evidence: This is concluded from the telomere elongation observed in heterozygous cells.

claim: TINF2 is a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene.
source: These data reveal TINF2 as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the combined genetic and cellular data.

claim: Inactivation of one TINF2 allele through truncation mutations results in inherited cancer predisposition with high penetrance and severity.
source: Inactivation of one TINF2 allele through truncation mutations results in inherited cancer predisposition with high penetrance and severity.
evidence: This is based on the clinical data from the families studied.

claim: The spectrum of cancers in the TINF2 families is broad, including breast cancer, colorectal cancer, thyroid cancer, and melanoma.
source: The spectrum of cancers in the TINF2 families studied here is broad, including breast cancer, colorectal cancer, thyroid cancer, and melanoma, and several patients had multiple independent malignancies.
evidence: This is documented in the clinical data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Several patients had multiple independent malignancies.
source: The spectrum of cancers in the TINF2 families studied here is broad, including breast cancer, colorectal cancer, thyroid cancer, and melanoma, and several patients had multiple independent malignancies.
evidence: This is documented in the clinical data presented in Figure 1.

claim: A recent report identified a TINF2 truncation mutation in a large family affected by thyroid cancer and melanoma.
source: Similarly, a recent report identified a TINF2 truncation mutation in a large family affected by thyroid cancer and melanoma (He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Inherited mutations in TINF2 can have two widely distinct outcomes.
source: It is remarkable that inherited mutations in TINF2 can have two widely distinct outcomes.
evidence: This is a comparison of the different phenotypes associated with different TINF2 mutations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in TINF2 cause cancer through aberrant telomere elongation.
source: While the loss-of-function mutations described here cause cancer through aberrant telomere elongation, missense mutations in the DC patch of TINF2 cause bone-marrow failure syndromes that are due to excessive telomere shortening.
evidence: This is concluded from the data presented in this study.

claim: Missense mutations in the DC patch of TINF2 cause bone-marrow failure syndromes that are due to excessive telomere shortening.
source: While the loss-of-function mutations described here cause cancer through aberrant telomere elongation, missense mutations in the DC patch of TINF2 cause bone-marrow failure syndromes that are due to excessive telomere shortening.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC-associated TINF2 mutations.

claim: The disparate outcomes of different TINF2 mutations reflect the dual role of TIN2.
source: These disparate outcomes reflect the dual role of TIN2, which uses its DC patch to promote telomere maintenance by telomerase, while keeping telomere length in check through its interaction with TRF1 and TPP1/POT1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the different phenotypes based on known TIN2 functions.

claim: TIN2 uses its DC patch to promote telomere maintenance by telomerase.
source: These disparate outcomes reflect the dual role of TIN2, which uses its DC patch to promote telomere maintenance by telomerase, while keeping telomere length in check through its interaction with TRF1 and TPP1/POT1.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about TIN2 function.

claim: TIN2 keeps telomere length in check through its interaction with TRF1 and TPP1/POT1.
source: These disparate outcomes reflect the dual role of TIN2, which uses its DC patch to promote telomere maintenance by telomerase, while keeping telomere length in check through its interaction with TRF1 and TPP1/POT1.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about TIN2 function and the data presented in this study.

claim: Telomere length at birth needs to be carefully controlled within a narrow range to prevent premature stem cell depletion and cancer.
source: Our genetic data underscore that telomere length at birth needs to be carefully controlled within a narrow range to prevent premature stem cell depletion on one hand and cancer on the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the contrasting phenotypes of different TINF2 mutations.

claim: The cancer-causing TINF2 mutations that create long germline telomeres without affecting telomere protection remove the ambiguity about whether long telomeres predispose to cancer.
source: The cancer-causing TINF2 mutations that create long germline telomeres without affecting telomere protection now remove the ambiguity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: It is extremely unlikely that genome instability contributes to tumorigenesis in the TINF2 cases.
source: In the TINF2 cases affected by inherited cancer predisposition, it is extremely unlikely that genome instability contributes to tumorigenesis since we have not detected loss of telomere protection or genome instability in heterozygous cell lines whose genotype mimic the patient status.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of telomere dysfunction in heterozygous cells.

claim: The simplest interpretation is that the patient's frequent malignancies are due to a failure in the telomere tumor suppressor pathway.
source: The simplest interpretation is that the patient's frequent malignancies are due to a failure in the telomere tumor suppressor pathway.
evidence: This is the main interpretation of the clinical and cellular data.

claim: There is no need to invoke genome instability as a cancer-promoting aspect of the POT1 mutations in familial cancer.
source: By extension, we argue that there is no need to invoke genome instability as a cancer-promoting aspect of the POT1 mutations in familial cancer.
evidence: This is an argument based on the findings with TINF2 mutations.

claim: The telomere elongation phenotype associated with the POT1 mutations is sufficient to explain the higher incidence of cancer in these families.
source: The data presented here argue that the telomere elongation phenotype associated with the POT1 mutations is sufficient to explain the higher incidence of cancer in these families.
evidence: This is an argument based on the findings with TINF2 mutations.

claim: Exceptionally long telomeres can lead to cancer predisposition.
source: According to our findings, exceptionally long telomeres can lead to cancer predisposition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The conclusion that long telomeres can lead to cancer predisposition is consistent with prior GWAS studies suggesting an effect of telomere length on cancer predisposition.
source: Our conclusion is consistent with prior GWAS studies suggesting an effect of telomere length on cancer predisposition (Rode et al., 2016; Telomeres Mendelian Randomization Collaboration et al., 2017; reviewed in McNally et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: It is pertinent to consider measuring telomere length in cancer-prone families lacking other genetic risk factors.
source: It is therefore pertinent to consider measuring telomere length in cancer-prone families lacking other genetic risk factors.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Caution is warranted with regard to efforts to interfere with the telomere shortening program in healthy individuals.
source: Our findings also suggest that caution is warranted with regard to efforts to interfere with the telomere shortening program in healthy individuals (Harley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The elongated telomeres associated with the inherited POT1 and TINF2 mutations suggest that the telomere length homeostasis observed in cultured cells reflect aspects of telomere length control in the human germline.
source: The elongated telomeres associated with the inherited POT1 and TINF2 mutations now suggest that the telomere length homeostasis observed in cultured cells reflect aspects of telomere length control in the human germline.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: The finding that cell culture systems reflect regulatory pathways observed in vivo should spur further in vitro experiments designed to illuminate how telomere length homeostasis is achieved.
source: The finding that cell culture systems reflect regulatory pathways observed in vivo should spur further in vitro experiments designed to illuminate how telomere length homeostasis is achieved.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the study findings.

claim: An important question to be addressed is why TIN2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control and which other shelterin components show this phenotype.
source: An important question to be addressed is why TIN2 is haploinsufficient for telomere length control and which other shelterin components show this phenotype.
evidence: This identifies an important question for future research.

claim: Shelterin components that are haploinsufficient for telomere length control but not for telomere protection are of particular interest since loss-of-function mutations in these genes could predispose to cancer.
source: Shelterin components that are haploinsufficient for telomere length control but not for telomere protection are of particular interest since loss-of-function mutations in these genes could predispose to cancer.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential significance of identifying other haploinsufficient shelterin components.

claim: TINF2 mutations lead to unusually long telomeres in the peripheral blood lymphocytes of the patients.
source: TINF2 mutations lead to unusually long telomeres in the peripheral blood lymphocytes of the patients reported here.
evidence: This is supported by the Flow-FISH and genomic blotting data.

claim: Long telomeres in peripheral blood lymphocytes likely reflect the long telomeres present in the bone marrow stem cells.
source: It is assumed that such long telomeres reflect the long telomeres present in the bone marrow stem cells since the number of divisions separating bone marrow stem cells from peripheral lymphocytes is too limited to allow the low level of telomerase in lymphocytes to extend the telomeres substantially.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biology of lymphocyte development.

claim: If the assumption about bone marrow stem cell telomere length is correct, the patients are likely born with unusually long telomeres in most of their stem cell compartments.
source: If this assumption is correct, the patients are likely born with unusually long telomeres in most of their stem cell compartments.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the assumption about bone marrow stem cell telomere length.

claim: The TINF2 mutations act by inappropriately elongating telomeres during early development.
source: These considerations lead us to propose that the TINF2 mutations act by inappropriately elongating telomeres during early development.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data and logical reasoning.

claim: Elongating telomeres during early development would elongate the normal sized telomeres inherited from the unaffected parent, preventing the timely onset of the Hayflick limit.
source: Importantly, such a process would elongate the normal sized telomeres inherited from the unaffected parent, preventing the timely onset of the Hayflick limit.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model explaining how the mutations lead to cancer predisposition.

claim: Telomerase is detectable in a number of embryonic tissues during the first and second trimester.
source: Since telomerase is detectable in a number of embryonic tissues during the first and second trimester (Wright et al., 1996), it is reasonable to assume that tens of cell divisions take place during which the enzyme can elongate telomeres unless it is restrained by the telomere length homeostasis pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that tens of cell divisions take place during early development during which telomerase can elongate telomeres unless restrained by the telomere length homeostasis pathway.
source: Since telomerase is detectable in a number of embryonic tissues during the first and second trimester (Wright et al., 1996), it is reasonable to assume that tens of cell divisions take place during which the enzyme can elongate telomeres unless it is restrained by the telomere length homeostasis pathway.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the presence of telomerase in embryonic tissues.

claim: The TINF2 mutations exert their cancer-promoting effects in the first weeks or months after fertilization.
source: We imagine that the TINF2 mutations exert their cancer-promoting effects in the first weeks or months after fertilization, resulting not only in long telomeres in the germline but also in all other stem cell compartments that are relevant to cancer development later in life.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for how the mutations lead to cancer predisposition.

claim: The TINF2 mutations result in long telomeres in the germline and in all other stem cell compartments relevant to cancer development.
source: We imagine that the TINF2 mutations exert their cancer-promoting effects in the first weeks or months after fertilization, resulting not only in long telomeres in the germline but also in all other stem cell compartments that are relevant to cancer development later in life.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for how the mutations lead to cancer predisposition.

claim: TINF2 would be a tumor suppressor gene with a very specific window of opportunity, exerting its effect early in development but not later.
source: According to this reasoning, TINF2 would be a tumor suppressor gene with a very specific window of opportunity, exerting its effect early in development but not later.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the proposed model.
